sections.h2: Where does a deed get recorded in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania?
sections.html:
Deeds for property in Cumberland County are recorded at the Recorder of Deeds office in the Historic Courthouse in Carlisle, at 1 Courthouse Square. The office keeps the permanent public record of deeds, mortgages and related papers for every borough and township in the county.

The office lists weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with some remote days, and it asks in-person visitors to book an appointment. Subdivision plans and notaries must have one. Call 717.240.6370 or email recorder@cumberlandcountypa.gov to set a time.

Most sellers never walk in. A title company or attorney handles the closing, prepares the deed and sends it for recording.

sections.h2: How much does the Cumberland County Recorder of Deeds charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
A deed costs $104.75 to record under the schedule that took effect November 17, 2025. That price already includes the $20 Uniform Parcel Identifier fee when one is needed, and each extra parcel adds $20.

Cumberland County recording fees, schedule effective November 17, 2025
DocumentFee
Deed$104.75
Mortgage$104.75
Satisfaction piece$78.25
Assignment of mortgage$78.25
Agreement of sale$78.25
Power of attorney with a parcel number$37.00
Notary public$34.00
Subdivision plan$47.00

Source: the Cumberland County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule. Deeds and mortgages add $2.00 for each page past four and $0.50 for each name past four. The fee sheet notes that the Commonwealth's Act 45 of 2025 raised the Criminal Justice Enhancement Account charge by $1, and deed and mortgage prices rose by that amount.

The county FAQ says the state legislature sets most fees, while the parcel identifier fee comes from a county ordinance. Attaching a Statement of Value adds $1.00.

sections.h2: How is realty transfer tax collected on a Cumberland County sale?
sections.html:
The recorder collects it when a taxable deed is presented. The county describes a 2% total on the price or value of the property interest: 1% goes to the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, and the other 1% is split evenly between the municipality and the school district.

The county keeps a small commission from each stream. According to its transfer tax page, that is 1% of the Commonwealth's share and 2% of the municipal distribution, and the money is passed on at the end of each month.

  • Pennsylvania's Department of Revenue says the buyer and the seller are both liable for the tax, so the purchase contract should say who pays.
  • Some transfers are exempt, including certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy. The recorder does not decide exemptions. Ask an attorney or the Department of Revenue.
  • Form REV-183, the Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value, is needed when claiming an exemption, when the price differs from the amount on the face of the deed, or when the deed is more than 30 days old.

On a $250,000 sale, a 2% total comes to $5,000 before any recording fees.

sections.h2: Can a Cumberland County deed be eRecorded?
sections.html:
Yes. The office accepts electronic recording, but only through three approved vendors: ePN, CSC and Simplifile. The county says most documents are now recorded electronically by attorneys and title companies.

Paper filings still work. Mail needs original signatures and notary stamps, because a photocopy cannot be recorded. If the payment is wrong, the office returns mailed documents without filing them, with one exception: an overage of $10 or less is kept and the document is recorded.

Checks are made payable to Recorder of Deeds. Credit cards run through Value Payment Systems, with a 2.25% convenience fee, a $2.50 minimum, and 3% on business cards. Cash refunds are not given.

sections.h2: How far back do Cumberland County deed records go?
sections.html:
The office has maintained a continuous record since 1750, so a title search can reach deeds from the colonial period. Its history page says the records came through the courthouse fire of 1845 unharmed and were hidden during the Confederate invasion of 1863.

Until 1929 every document was copied by hand into canvas bound books. Typed books followed, and separate index books for deeds, mortgages and miscellaneous papers were kept until December 1993, when indexing was computerized. The office stopped making paper books in 2001, and in November 2017 the old books moved from the courthouse to the County Archives.

Records back to 1750 can be searched online through Landex at any hour, or at the Recorder's office on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Searches run by name, not by address. To find the owner of a particular parcel, use the Tax Assessment Office or the county's GIS Property Mapper.

sections.h2: What should a seller in Cumberland County check around recording?
sections.html:
Confirm that every lien on the property is cleared, because the Recorder only holds mortgages and secured transactions. The county's FAQ says judgment liens, municipal liens and state tax liens are filed with the Cumberland County Prothonotary instead, so a title search needs to cover both offices.

  • The lender records a satisfaction piece when a mortgage is paid, and the homeowner does not receive a new deed.
  • Staff cannot run title searches or give legal advice. Use a title searcher, an abstract company or an attorney.
  • Recorded plans from the early 1900s onward may be on file, and a plan reference often appears in the deed's property description.
  • A veteran's DD214 can be recorded, and a certified copy is free if the original is lost. Military discharge records are not open to public viewing.

The county's Tax Claim Bureau sells delinquent properties in an online upset sale, and its 2026 sale terms state that transfer tax and recording fees are added to the winning bid. The tax equals the assessed value times the Common Level Ratio Factor, times 2%.

sections.h2: What does Cumberland County look like for a seller?
sections.html:
The courthouse and the Recorder's office are in Carlisle. The Census Bureau counts 277,270 residents as of July 2025, up 6.9% from the 2020 base, spread over 545.48 square miles.

QuickFacts lists 114,465 housing units, an owner occupied rate of 71.3% and a median owner occupied value of $277,600 for 2020 to 2024. Median gross rent is $1,249, and median household income is $87,494. The county issued 745 building permits in 2025.

The 2026 county tax rate is 2.875 mills, with municipal and school rates added on top. Total real estate rates on the county's rate sheet range from about 15.95 mills in Hampden Township to about 27.27 mills in Newville Borough, so the tax on a house depends heavily on which district it sits in.

faqs.q: What is the fee to record a deed in Cumberland County?
faqs.a: The fee is $104.75 under the schedule effective November 17, 2025, including the $20 parcel identifier fee when required. Extra pages past four cost $2.00 each and extra names past four cost $0.50 each. Transfer tax is paid separately.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax when a house sells in Cumberland County?
faqs.a: The buyer and seller are both legally liable for the Pennsylvania tax, so the purchase agreement decides who pays it in practice. The county collects a 2% total at recording, split among the state, the municipality and the school district.

faqs.q: Does the Recorder of Deeds search my title for me?
faqs.a: No. Staff are not bonded or permitted to run title searches or give legal advice. They can show you how to use the public computers. A title searcher, abstract company or attorney does the search, and records are indexed by name.

faqs.q: Do I get a new deed after I pay off my mortgage?
faqs.a: No. The lender records a satisfaction piece showing the mortgage is paid, and your original deed stays the same. If you need a copy of your deed, order it through Landex or email the Recorder's office for an electronic copy.

faqs.q: Can I record documents by mail or online?
faqs.a: Yes to both, with limits. Mail needs original signatures, notary stamps and the exact fee. Online recording goes through ePN, CSC or Simplifile only. Subdivision plans and notary filings require an appointment instead.
